A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Preble/E2 research. Their text, figures, tables and algorithms support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 moves substantial existing material into appendices A–C, which were included in the comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original workload analyses, GPU profiling, serving-performance comparisons, component ablations and scheduler-throughput measurements in Sections 3 and 5.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results in Section 4 and the appendices, and adds performance comparisons using a newer SGLang version in Appendix C.

M1.justification: The hierarchical E2 architecture remains, but eviction cost changes from accumulated request recomputation costs to node-prefill costs weighted by normalized hit frequencies. History H changes from a request-count window to a time window. Algorithm 1 also corrects its exploitation condition to missed_len < cached_len, matching the existing prose; this correction alone does not establish an implementation change.

E1.justification: Both versions use Toolbench, ALFWorld, APPS programming, NExT-QA, LooGLE and the Azure arrival trace, including mixed workloads and skewed tool popularity. The newer-backend experiments reuse existing tasks rather than adding dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Oracle partition is removed from the main end-to-end comparisons and the vLLM experiment. The ablation reference also changes from Oracle partition to round-robin SGLang. Appendix C adds an evaluated SGLang v0.3 configuration with an updated FlashInfer kernel. These changes substantially alter the comparison set.

E3.justification: The main models, GPU configurations, arrival-process framework and latency metrics remain. However, Figure 3 revises request-rate sweeps relative to v1 Figure 7, including LooGLE, and Appendix C adds experiments with newer SGLang/FlashInfer software configurations. These are reported evaluation-setting changes, without establishing which existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The component ablation remains but changes its starting comparator. v2 adds backend-version robustness evidence in Figure 12, reports insensitivity to different history-window lengths, and reports a network-bottleneck check. The smaller, 200-tool scheduler-throughput case from v1 is omitted.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains the same means and standard deviations for workload properties. Neither version reports performance uncertainty through repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The central performance evidence changes: v2 Figure 3 revises several latency curves and result points from v1 Figure 7, while Figure 12 adds Toolbench and LooGLE results with the newer backend. Oracle-partition results and the 634 requests/s scheduler result are removed. The mixed-workload results remain unchanged. Revised configurations and rate sweeps prevent treating all curve differences as same-setting gains.

T1.justification: The eviction-cost definition changes substantively: v1 uses request counts for Nj, whereas v2 defines Nj as a normalized historical hit frequency in Mi = sum_j PTj × Nj. This changes the mathematical weighting, beyond notation. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v2 drops the introductory oracle-partition superiority claim and the listed contribution of identifying three new distributed-systems challenges. The central claims about E2, the first distributed prompt-sharing serving system, and the headline average/p99 latency improvement ranges remain.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the broad hundreds-to-thousands-of-GPUs scalability extrapolation with an estimate of 70–391 A100 GPUs and explicit decoding-speed assumptions. It adds explanations involving backend optimizations and vLLM scheduling delay, while removing oracle-performance explanations and the shared-system-prompt explanation for programming results.

D1.justification: v2 replaces a future code-release promise with a reported public repository location, specifies backend versions, supplies a three-minute H default and clarifies server topology. It removes Table 1's exact request counts, CPU and source-line details, and the Azure replay's 0.7× timing adjustment and sampling explanation. Omitted details do not establish changed execution settings.

R1.justification: The extensive traditional stateful-systems comparison and graph-partitioning positioning are removed. v2 concentrates on LLM serving, adds a substantive comparison with Prompt Cache, and introduces references to MemServe, Mooncake, Déjàvu and production prompt caching. This materially reshapes the research positioning beyond citation-format or publication-metadata updates.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. The detailed workload study moves to Appendix A, profiling to Appendix B, algorithms to appendix pages and backend comparisons to Appendix C. Related work moves after evaluation, substantially changing the narrative structure.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to one, with extensive figure and algorithm relocation. v2 adds a compact workload-summary diagram and a backend-version comparison figure, redraws comparison plots, removes Table 1's request-count column and adds local-scheduler pseudocode. Figure 11 introduces an inconsistent SGLang legend for an experiment described as vLLM.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects the exploitation pseudocode, improves parts of the method description, provides code-access information and tests a newer backend. However, removing oracle-partition comparisons weakens evidence against a prompt-aware placement alternative, while omitted workload counts and Azure replay details reduce reproducibility. Figure 11 also introduces a baseline-label inconsistency. These substantive gains and losses leave the net quality direction uncertain.
